title: Air India to Restore Most International Routes From September After Summer-Long Cuts
excerpt: Routes to Chicago and Washington Dulles remain suspended, but the Tata-owned carrier says the rest of its global network will bounce back after three months of deep reductions.
body:
• Air India will restore most suspended and reduced international flights from September 2026, ending a three-month network rationalization prompted by airspace restrictions and record jet fuel prices.
  • Routes to Chicago O'Hare and Washington Dulles will remain suspended due to limited aircraft availability, affecting diaspora communities in the Midwest and DC metro area.
  • The pullback was the broadest since the Tata Group took over Air India in 2022, with cuts spanning North America, Europe, Australia, and Southeast Asia.
  • Despite the summer reductions, the airline maintained over 1,200 international flights per month across five continents.

Air India will restore the bulk of its international network from September after a three-month rationalization that saw the Tata-owned carrier cut or suspend dozens of routes across North America, Europe, Australia, and Asia.

The confirmation came from Nipun Aggarwal, Air India's Chief Commercial and Transformation Officer, at a tourism conference organized by the Federation of Associations in Indian Tourism & Hospitality (FAITH) in New Delhi. Aggarwal said the airline had reduced capacity only between June and August and confirmed that September flights had remained available for booking throughout the period.

What Was Cut

The summer rationalization carved deep into Air India's international schedule. In North America, the Delhi-Chicago route was fully suspended, Delhi-San Francisco dropped from 10 to seven weekly flights, Delhi-Toronto fell from 10 to five weekly services through July before increasing to daily in August, and Delhi-Vancouver went from seven to five weekly flights. Mumbai-New York JFK and Delhi-Newark services were temporarily suspended, though Mumbai-Newark was boosted from three to seven weekly flights to partially compensate.

European routes took significant hits. Delhi-Paris was halved from 14 to seven weekly flights, while services from Delhi to Copenhagen, Milan, Vienna, Zurich, and Rome each lost one to two weekly frequencies. In Australia, both Delhi-Melbourne and Delhi-Sydney were cut from daily service to four flights per week.

Southeast Asian routes saw some of the sharpest reductions. Delhi-Singapore dropped from 24 to 14 weekly flights, Mumbai-Singapore from 14 to seven, and Delhi-Bangkok from 28 to 21. Delhi-Shanghai, Chennai-Singapore, and Delhi-Malé were fully suspended through August.

Why the Cuts Happened

Air India attributed the changes to a combination of continued airspace restrictions over certain regions and record-high jet fuel prices for international operations. Aviation industry publication Skift described the move as "one of the broadest schedule pullbacks the airline has announced since the Tata Group took over in 2022."

"The adjustments have been made in response to continued airspace restrictions over certain regions and record high jet fuel prices for international operations, which significantly impact the commercial viability of certain planned services."

— Air India

The airline emphasized that even during the reduced period, it continued to operate more than 1,200 international flights per month spanning five continents — 33 weekly flights to North America, 47 to Europe, 57 to the UK, eight to Australia, 158 across the Far East, Southeast Asia, and SAARC regions, and seven to Mauritius.

What Stays Grounded

While most routes are set to return, two notable gaps remain. Services to Chicago O'Hare and Washington Dulles will continue to be suspended because of limited aircraft availability, according to Aggarwal. The continued absence of these two routes is significant for the Indian diaspora — Chicago's metropolitan area is home to one of the largest Indian communities in the United States, and the Washington DC area served by Dulles hosts a major concentration of Indian tech workers, government professionals, and diplomats.

What NRI Travelers Should Know

For diaspora travelers who deferred summer plans or dealt with rebookings, the September restoration is a relief. Routes like Delhi-San Francisco, heavily used by Bay Area-based Indian tech workers, and Delhi-Toronto, critical for Canada's large Indian community, will return to their full weekly schedules.

Passengers whose bookings were affected during the June-August window were offered re-accommodation on alternative Air India flights, free date changes, or full refunds. Air India said it would continue to work with regulators and airport authorities to restore full capacity but cautioned that further adjustments could follow if extraordinary operating conditions persist.
